meta_desc: Master prime factorization, LCM and GCF for Grade 6 with factor trees, exponents and a simple GCF-vs-LCM rule, plus a free 8-question quiz and worksheet.
excerpt: A factor tree turns a scary number like 84 into a tidy string of primes, and once a Grade 6 student can write that string, GCF and LCM stop being guesswork. Here is the method I teach, step by step, with a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Give a Grade 6 student two numbers like 24 and 36 and ask for the GCF, and most will start listing every factor of each, hunting for the biggest one they share. It works — until the numbers get bigger and the lists get long and someone misses a factor. There is a faster, more reliable way, and it all rests on one skill: prime factorization. Once a student can break a number into its primes, prime factorization, LCM and GCF for Grade 6 stop being three separate headaches and become one connected method. This is skill practice — the how, not the theory of what a factor is.

I have taught this to plenty of eleven-year-olds, including a few who were convinced they were ‘bad at maths’. The factor tree is what usually turns them around, because it feels like a puzzle rather than a rule to memorise.

Start with a factor tree

A factor tree breaks a number into two factors, then breaks those factors again, until every branch ends in a prime number (a number whose only factors are 1 and itself: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, and so on). Take 84. Split it into 4 × 21. Neither is prime, so keep going: 4 becomes 2 × 2, and 21 becomes 3 × 7. Every branch now ends in a prime, so you stop.

Reading off the leaves of the tree, 84 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 7. Here is the reassuring part I always point out: it does not matter where you start. Split 84 as 2 × 42 instead, and you land on exactly the same four primes. Every number has one, and only one, prime factorization — a fact that quietly does a lot of heavy lifting later.

Write it neatly with exponents

Once the primes are found, tidy them up using exponents. Instead of 2 × 2 × 3 × 7, write 2² × 3 × 7. For a number like 72 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3, exponent form is 2³ × 3². This is not just for neatness — the exponent form is what makes GCF and LCM almost mechanical.

Prime factorization, LCM and GCF for Grade 6: the payoff

Here is where the single skill pays off three times over. Write both numbers in prime-factor form, line up the primes, and read off two answers using two small rules. Let us use 24 and 36.

  • 24 = 2³ × 3
  • 36 = 2² × 3²

GCF (also called HCF) is the product of the common primes, each taken to its lowest power. Both share a 2 and a 3. The lowest power of 2 is 2²; the lowest power of 3 is 3¹. So GCF = 2² × 3 = 12.

LCM is the product of all primes that appear in either number, each taken to its highest power. The highest power of 2 is 2³; the highest power of 3 is 3². So LCM = 2³ × 3² = 72.

No listing, no guessing. Just line up the primes and pick lowest-and-common for GCF, all-and-highest for LCM.

A quick memory hook

Which primes?Which power?
GCF (HCF)Only the shared onesLowest
LCMAll of themHighest

I tell students: GCF is greedy about what it shares but shy about size (common primes, smallest powers), while LCM invites everyone and takes the biggest (all primes, largest powers). Silly, but it sticks.

A worked example with three primes

Try 90 and 84. Factorise: 90 = 2 × 3² × 5, and 84 = 2² × 3 × 7. The shared primes are 2 and 3, so GCF = 2¹ × 3¹ = 6. For the LCM, gather every prime that shows up — 2, 3, 5 and 7 — at its highest power: 2² × 3² × 5 × 7 = 1260. Notice the 5 and the 7 each appear in only one number; they still join the LCM but never the GCF. That asymmetry trips students up, so point it out.

When do I use GCF and when LCM?

Knowing how to compute both is only half the skill. The other half is choosing the right one, and word problems rarely say which. Here is the rule of thumb I give:

  • Use GCF when you are splitting or grouping things into the largest equal parts — cutting a 24 cm and a 36 cm ribbon into equal pieces with none left over, or making identical gift bags from 24 pens and 36 erasers. The answer is smaller than the numbers.
  • Use LCM when you are looking for when things line up again — two buses leaving every 24 and 36 minutes, meeting again after 72 minutes. The answer is bigger than the numbers.

One honest caveat: this rhyme is a guide, not a law. A handful of problems need both, and a few are worded to trick you. When a student is unsure, I ask a single question — ‘are we breaking things down, or waiting for them to meet up?’ Down means GCF; meet means LCM. That question alone clears up most of the confusion.

Common slip-ups to watch for

Three mistakes come up again and again. First, forgetting that 1 is not prime, so it never belongs on a factor tree. Second, mixing up the powers — taking the highest power for GCF or the lowest for LCM. Third, dropping a prime that appears in only one number when building the LCM. A tidy, exponent-form layout catches all three, which is exactly why I insist on it.

quiz.title: Grade 6 Prime Factorization, LCM & GCF Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on factor trees, prime factorization with exponents, GCF and LCM. Solve each on paper, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 6 prime factorization, LCM and GCF

questions.q: What is the prime factorization of 60?
questions.explanation: 60 = 2 × 30 = 2 × 2 × 15 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5, which is 2² × 3 × 5. Every leaf must be prime, so 15 and 10 cannot be final answers.

questions.q: Which of these numbers is prime?
questions.explanation: 29 has only 1 and 29 as factors. 21 = 3 × 7, 27 = 3³, and 33 = 3 × 11.

questions.q: The GCF of two numbers uses which primes and powers?
questions.explanation: GCF (HCF) is the product of the primes shared by both numbers, each taken to its lowest power.

questions.q: Given 24 = 2³ × 3 and 36 = 2² × 3², what is the GCF?
questions.explanation: Common primes are 2 and 3. Lowest powers: 2² and 3¹. GCF = 2² × 3 = 12.

questions.q: Given 24 = 2³ × 3 and 36 = 2² × 3², what is the LCM?
questions.explanation: Take all primes at their highest power: 2³ and 3². LCM = 2³ × 3² = 8 × 9 = 72.

questions.q: What is 72 written in exponent form?
Two buses leave a stop together, one every 15 minutes and one every 20 minutes. After how many minutes do they leave together again?
questions.explanation: This is a ‘meet up again’ problem, so use LCM. 15 = 3 × 5, 20 = 2² × 5, LCM = 2² × 3 × 5 = 60.

questions.q: You have 18 pens and 24 pencils and want to make identical kits with none left over. What is the greatest number of kits?
questions.explanation: This is a ‘split into equal groups’ problem, so use GCF. 18 = 2 × 3², 24 = 2³ × 3, GCF = 2 × 3 = 6.

faq.q: What is the difference between GCF and HCF?
faq.a: None — they are two names for the same thing. GCF (greatest common factor) is the term used in many textbooks, while HCF (highest common factor) is common in Indian and NCERT-aligned materials. Both mean the largest number that divides two or more numbers exactly.

faq.q: Why write prime factorization with exponents?
faq.a: Exponent form (like 2³ × 3²) is compact and, more importantly, makes GCF and LCM almost mechanical: you just compare the powers of each shared or total prime. It also prevents miscounting how many times a prime appears.

faq.q: Is there a quick way to remember GCF versus LCM?
faq.a: Yes. For GCF, use only the primes both numbers share, each at its lowest power. For LCM, use every prime that appears in either number, each at its highest power. In word problems, ‘splitting into equal groups’ means GCF; ‘when do they line up again’ means LCM.

faq.q: Does it matter how I split the first branch of a factor tree?
faq.a: No. You can start 84 as 4 × 21 or 2 × 42 or 6 × 14 — you always end up with the same set of primes. Every whole number greater than 1 has exactly one prime factorization.
